title: Headwear Manager by Day, 3D Architect by Night: Inside @collin3D’s Hyper-Realistic World
content:
## ![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202605/42caea55740d4db4aff0920a708d4c0b/images/b73600ed9faf44f8a715dfc05f20a404cvl_2026_may_userspotlight.jpg)_By day, Honolulu-based Collin (_[_@collin3D_](https://www.instagram.com/collin3d/) _) is a headwear design manager; by night, he crafts hyper-realistic 3D fashion in CLO. Obsessed with the tiny imperfections that bring digital garments to life, his virtual fits easily trick the eye. In this interview, Collin drops his texturing secrets and reveals why ditching Pinterest for real-world inspiration is his ultimate design cheat code._  


* * *

![beff152eb4934a0fa847a669ba9b4294](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202604/42caea55740d4db4aff0920a708d4c0b/images/beff152eb4934a0fa847a669ba9b4294image%20%2835%29%20%281%29.png)

**Q. Can you introduce yourself and share a little about your background and current focus in 3D design?**

Hello, my name is Collin and I am a 3D designer based in Honolulu, Hawaii. I work full time as a design manager at a premium headwear company. In my free time, I dive into the 3D world creating personal 3D fashion designs as well as 3D modeling and animating for many other brands.

**Q. How did you start your journey in 3D fashion, and what made you choose CLO as your primary tool?**

My 3D fashion journey started when I was creating clothing cad designs in illustrator for a company I used to work for. Before learning CLO, I was constantly looking for ways to express my ideas and fashion designs. In addition to cad design I was doing simple sketches, modifying existing garments in photoshop, and even trying to sculpt the clothes in different 3D modeling programs. However, I wasn’t ever able to get anything to a point of what I was happy with nor envisioned. I almost started going crazy with all the things I wanted to create and not having a way to express it. I started to research other options and that’s when I quickly ran into CLO.

![a44aa16988f24143bfa6d12d4344d003](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202604/42caea55740d4db4aff0920a708d4c0b/images/a44aa16988f24143bfa6d12d4344d003Screenshot%202026-03-12%20at%201.07.36%E2%80%AFPM.png)

![bfd696c0175c4fac91ad0d970f8992d4](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202604/42caea55740d4db4aff0920a708d4c0b/images/bfd696c0175c4fac91ad0d970f8992d4Screenshot%202026-03-12%20at%201.16.08%E2%80%AFPM.png)

After the steep learning curve, I was so excited to be able to create the designs that I have been keeping in my head for so long. I think one of the worst feelings as an artist is being overwhelmed with things you want to create and not having the proper medium to bring those creations to life. I am happy that CLO has been my medium thus far to showcase my art.

**Q. Looking at your posts from the past year, the realistic textures and fabric details stand out. What do you focus on most when creating complex materials like knits or denim?**

Thank you for the compliment. This is probably the most time consuming part of my work. I try so hard to make all of my renders look like real life pieces to a point where some people might even question if it is a real garment. Real garments in fact are what I focus on to try and achieve this look. I am literally staring at real life pieces looking at say the way nylon wrinkles on the seam, the way denim puckers on the cuffs, or even the little tiny pebbles or imperfections on leather jackets. When you compare a lot of 3D clothing renders and real life pieces, you can often spot the 3D render because of how “perfect” it is. The imperfections of human error and real life material is what I’m looking to capture. Little details like this I think help 3D renders look a little closer to reality.

![3af43c46458c4590b4219edc4f95b7d4](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202604/42caea55740d4db4aff0920a708d4c0b/images/3af43c46458c4590b4219edc4f95b7d4close%20%281%29.png)

![a2b3eae4beac460e9fe4f3c58e6aa8b0](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202604/42caea55740d4db4aff0920a708d4c0b/images/a2b3eae4beac460e9fe4f3c58e6aa8b0DiorBack2.png)

**Q. Your work goes beyond showcasing garments; the mood and lighting create a distinct atmosphere. Do you have a specific philosophy or preferred setup when rendering your scenes?**

My render setups are simply “if I owned a clothing brand, how would I want to showcase it?” These real life photoshoot environments are the kind of imagery I want to create. It’s much easier to incorporate unique elements like statement couches or distinctive plants into a shoot in 3D than it is in real life. There are virtually no limitations. When it comes to the lighting, I personally try to add as little lights as possible. I want the main light source to come from different HDRIs so that the end result looks very natural and the clothing isn’t blown out by certain studio lights.

  
**Q. Out of all your projects, which one is your favorite or most memorable? Please tell us why.**

I think my favorite and most memorable project I did was honestly [_my first ever clothing post_](https://www.instagram.com/reels/CrPhD9eu9M2/) which was a concept I did for a brand and designer I looked up to for a long time. I created 100s of designs before this, but I was so excited that I finally created a product I felt happy showcasing. Looking back, it was just a simple logo puffer jacket, and since then my designs have become far more detailed and intricate. However, that outfit definitely started the journey and I still remember the feeling of posting my first 3D clothing design.

![68cb777d639a4e21b01e30fc3aa52fcb](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202604/42caea55740d4db4aff0920a708d4c0b/images/68cb777d639a4e21b01e30fc3aa52fcbFinalMain%20%281%29.png)

**Q. Which CLO tools or features do you find most valuable in your design process?**

I think it would be disrespectful to CLO to choose only a couple tools or features that are my favorite lol. Just the fact that I have a digital sewing machine at my finger tips where I can create any clothing item that can be translated to a real life garment is what makes me love CLO.

**Q. Given the high quality of your work, it seems you use other software alongside CLO. Could you briefly describe your typical workflow combining different tools?**

I use CLO to create all my base clothing designs. I render everything in Blender. My texturing is all over the place haha. Hard to explain my entire process via words, but I use a heavy mix of photoshop and texture stacking with nodes in blender. I look forward to other ways of texturing in the future like substance painter and even more integrations that CLO introduces.

**Q. What do you struggle with the most in the creative process, and how do you deal with the feeling of being overwhelmed by wanting to create so many designs?**

That’s honestly the thing I struggle with the most. I have so many pictures, notes, mood boards, and random ideas saved on things I want to create. One of the hardest parts is just finding the time to actually bring all those ideas to life.  
The only way I’ve been able to somewhat deal with the feeling of being overwhelmed is by fully immersing myself in whatever design I’m currently working on. I try my best to focus only on ways to improve the piece in front of me instead of constantly thinking about the next idea.

![dd94481d00dd44a4998a83e75f7cc1cc](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202604/42caea55740d4db4aff0920a708d4c0b/images/dd94481d00dd44a4998a83e75f7cc1ccIMG_7445%20%281%29.png)  
I think a lot of people end up chasing the algorithm, posting as many designs as possible because they believe quantity is more important than quality. I know I probably should post more often too, but sometimes you’ll notice there’s a month gap between my projects. That’s because I treat every design as if it’s actually going to be produced. I keep making small adjustments all the way up until the day I post it.

![9d7aa99ec85443d2a78d25edee1b6e2d](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202604/42caea55740d4db4aff0920a708d4c0b/images/9d7aa99ec85443d2a78d25edee1b6e2dimage%20%2833%29%20%281%29.png)  
Sometimes I’ll look back and realize that if I had posted a design any earlier, before those last minute changes, it would’ve been completely different. Those small tweaks, while not trying to overdo it, can make a huge difference.

For any artist who feels overwhelmed, try to see it as a positive sign. It usually means you truly love to create. Use that energy as fuel and channel it into making as much as you can.

**Q. What advice would you give to students or beginners who are just starting their journey in 3D fashion?**

Design what you love. These programs can get overwhelming and complicated enough to make you want to quit. The only way to push through is by creating pieces and working in categories you’re genuinely passionate about. When I first started, it felt like my entire life revolved around improving my renders. I watched endless YouTube videos and spent hours researching just to fix one small glitch. I thought about my renders, before bed, on walks, in the shower, etc. If you’re not truly obsessed with it, this probably isn’t the space for you and you will eventually get burned out. I believe that 3D fashion is the future and if you are able to conceptualize your ideas in this way, you will stand out against the rest because you aren’t on real world timelines like factories, manual sewing, fitting errors / etc. Also, I think finding someone you can bounce your ideas off of is extremely helpful. I think as designers when we stare at a screen and one design for hours on end, sometimes we need a fresh set of eyes. In my posts you will often see me tag one of my best friends, who runs a page called wonder years studios. We are constantly hashing out new ideas with each other and it helps me tremendously to see something new that I might have missed.

![8345592e8c7d45b7baac48532afd846f](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202604/42caea55740d4db4aff0920a708d4c0b/images/8345592e8c7d45b7baac48532afd846fmoodboard%20%282%29%20%281%29.png)

The last piece of advice I’d give is to put the phone down. This industry is flooded with the same designs, slightly tweaked again and again. I’m not saying I’m not guilty of it too, but my strongest ideas usually come when I step away from social media and screens. Go outside. Pay attention to the world around you. Just going for walks can spark new ideas. For example, these pictures (added below) were from my walk today. The way the rain dried on the pavement looked like it could become a new texture for a jacket. The base shape of this palm tree felt like it could inspire a whole new silhouette. Just looking up in real life can really elevate your designs to something original instead of another Pinterest trendy sweatsuit that looks like everything else.

**Q. Is there a new style or project you’re excited to try next? What are your future plans?**

I wouldn’t say there’s one specific project I’m most excited to work on next. I have so many ideas that I’m eager to share as I continue to grow. Ultimately, I’d love to take my journey toward creating more real world pieces. It’s definitely an expensive process, but I’m passionate about turning my content into something that begins with a sketch, moves into the sewing process in CLO, includes the texture rendering, and then captures the behind the scenes production of the final product coming to life. I think this type of process would create in depth content that really highlights how capable these 3D programs are. Whether that happens through collaborations with other brands or by launching something of my own, I’m open to wherever the journey leads. More than anything, I’d love to see my virtual designs brought into the real world and worn in everyday life.
content_description: Showcasing Honolulu-based 3D designer Collin’s journey, techniques, and philosophy behind creating hyper-realistic digital fashion using CLO, blending real-world inspiration with cutting-edge virtual garment design.

title: Importing CSV Files For Auto Pattern Drafting And Auto Grading
content:
Importing CSV Files For Auto Pattern Drafting And Auto Grading

I watched the Official Tutorial of the New Features, Deep Dives and New Pattern Drafter Features.

I did not see explanation of Auto Grading and importing CSV Files for Auto Pattern Drafting.

Question 1) How to import CSV files including Trousers measurements for Auto Pattern Drafting?

Question 2) As far as I understand we can Auto Grade the patterns from Measurement Tables we import as CSV files etc.

How’s that gonna be?

Question 3) How to draw a trousers without darts with Pattern Drafter?

I can not enter 0 as dart value.

### Community Post Comments:
Comment 1: Hi, you can open CSV files inside the drafter by clicking on the folder icon. The calculator for trousers with elastic waistband does not contain darts, in opposite to the one for slacks.
Reply 1: Additional note - this is taken from a write-up by Ariel: It needs to be a specific CSV. The best way to do this is to first add how many sizes you want. Then click the floppy disc save icon after the initial specs are in, and this will save out the .csv spec sheet. Once you have the spec sheet you can open it in Excel, input all your size data. Then open this CSV in CLO.
content_description: This webpage provides guidance on importing CSV files for auto pattern drafting and grading, including troubleshooting tips for drafting trousers without darts using the Pattern Drafter tool.

title: Macbook - Clo3D Can Not Import DXF Or PDF Files
content:
Macbook - Clo3D Neither Import DXF Nor PDF Files

I drawn the patterns on Affinity Designer then exported

A) DXF (preseve vectors)

B) PDF (default)

In Clo3D I try “File - Import”

A) For DXF Files

This software supports DXF-AAMA or DXF-ASTM file formats only. As the loaded Pattern file is not in DXF-AAMA or DXF-ASTM format, all lines will be converted to Baselines.

B) For PDF files

This is an unsupported file type. When saving the Al file, please check the option "Create PDF Compatible File".

title: Macbook Error - Clo3D Not Opened
content:
When I try to install and then open Clo3D I get this error;

Clo3D Not Opened

Apple could not verify “X” is free of malware that may harm your Mac or compromise your privacy.

And the app won’t initiate.

How can I fix this?

### Community Post Comments:
Comment 1: I'm sure It does not contain a virus. But I wanted to learn how to make Macbook open Clo3d in this case?
Reply 1: An mentioned at my reply You may need to look at your computers security settings.If you need further help you will need to reach out to tech support directly though a ticket-https://connect.clo-set.com/community/post/ddeb8879fd0a46689b03b318b892738b

Comment 2: below answer comes directly from our Tech TeamCLO does not contain viruses or malware. We scan the CLO software with world-class security solutions before and after distribution.  Please make sure to download the CLO installer distributed by the official CLO website. We do not guarantee installers distributed from places other than the CLO official website. If your Windows Defender or UAC restricts the installation of CLO, please review their detailed settings. If necessary, you may need to slightly lower the security monitoring level for the CLO software. Additionally, certain antivirus software or even web communication monitoring programs like AdBlock may falsely detect CLO software as a malicious app; therefore, please try temporarily disabling them when installing CLO.
content_description: This web page provides solutions to resolve the "Apple could not verify" error preventing Clo3D from opening on a Mac.

I am a regular user of CLO 3D and I would like to suggest an improvement regarding the **"Pattern Annotation"** tool.

**Tal**

title: Wave Pleat Manipulation
content:
## ![2acc1f34500c4bb79c7f7173aa3b7c5a](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202605/99c687456bf74aaaa625aeba403a1668/images/2acc1f34500c4bb79c7f7173aa3b7c5aPleats_Custom_View_4.png)

* * *

## _Wave Pleat Manipulation in CLO3D_

• Wave pleat manipulation is a hybrid technique combining accordion pleating and smocking logic, where pleats are selectively “locked” using offset constraints. In CLO3D, this effect is achieved through fold arrangements and strategic tack placement, allowing designers to simulate complex textile textures in a controllable, procedural way.

![08028d859bfe4177a9e6a047378e512b](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202605/99c687456bf74aaaa625aeba403a1668/images/08028d859bfe4177a9e6a047378e512bPleats_Custom_View_2.png)![d017cd9ca3cb4a81ae57d5234b300eef](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202605/99c687456bf74aaaa625aeba403a1668/images/d017cd9ca3cb4a81ae57d5234b300eefPleats_Custom_View_1.png)

To create a wave pleat manipulation:  
• Start with a rectangular pattern and apply Accordion pleats to generate evenly spaced vertical pleats. 

• Using the Tack tool, connect points across the pleats but offset each row alternately (left–right shift).

• After simulating, refine the result by adjusting:

\- Particle Distance (5–10) for sharper folds

\- Bending stiffness to maintain structure

\- Tack placement for more natural variation

![1ad2241ce38a451ebe16a94605436668](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202605/99c687456bf74aaaa625aeba403a1668/images/1ad2241ce38a451ebe16a94605436668image.png)

Optionally, use Strengthen or partial freezing to stabilize the form.

### Community Post Comments:
Comment 1: it's a very clean work!!!!👍🏻
Reply 1: thank youu 🌷🌷
content_description: This web page explains how to create and refine wave pleat manipulations in CLO3D using accordion pleats, tack tools, and simulation adjustments for realistic textile textures.

title: Gathers at centre front
content:
Dear all, I’m stuck on one issue. I would like to create gathers along the center front seam. Both pattern pieces are opened up at the center front. How can I gather this excess fullness down to a specific length?

Many thanks & Best Tina

![d9ac4a288c674008aef547a1f7529a71](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202604/3453fc42a3a64d93b029fd478e28a48f/images/d9ac4a288c674008aef547a1f7529a711.jpg)![6e2186c12abf432abf765368ae3374e5](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202604/3453fc42a3a64d93b029fd478e28a48f/images/6e2186c12abf432abf765368ae3374e52.jpg)

### Community Post Comments:
Comment 1: Great Start!. The easiest way would be to apply elastic in the Property editor.Use the Edit PatternTool and Select the 2 lines that would be sewn and gathered, Then in the Property Editor turn on Elastic. This is a Ratio method for the elastic, so you can start at 80 and then increase or decrease as needed to get the gathers
content_description: Provide guidance on creating gathers along an opened center front seam to manage excess fabric and achieve a desired length in garment pattern pieces.
